# Organizing: Setting Up the Right Buckets

## Core Organizing Principle

Being organized means where something is matches what it means to you. If you decide to keep something as reference and put it where reference material belongs, that's organized. Your physical organization system must be better than your mental one for your mind to let go of lower-level thinking.

## The Seven Basic Categories

Seven primary types of things to keep track of:

1. A Projects list
2. Project support material
3. Calendar actions and information
4. Next Actions lists
5. A Waiting For list
6. Reference material
7. A Someday/Maybe list

### Hard Edges

Categories must be kept visually, physically, and psychologically separate. If you allow things of different meanings into the same grouping, you go psychologically numb to the contents. If you put items on Next Actions lists that need to go on the calendar, you won't trust your calendar. Projects you're not acting on must go on Someday/Maybe.

### Lists and Folders

Once you know what you need to track, lists and folders are sufficient tools. A list could be: a file folder with separate notes, an actual list on paper, or an inventory in software.

## Organizing Action Reminders

After emptying your in-tray, you'll have twenty to seventy or more pending items representing longer-than-two-minute actions that cannot be delegated.

### Calendar Actions

The calendar should show only the "hard landscape." There are two kinds of actions: those that must be done on a certain day and/or at a particular time, and those that just need to be done as soon as you can. Resist putting on the calendar things you'd like to get done but that might not happen. You need to trust your calendar as sacred territory.

### Organizing Actions by Context

The best way to be reminded of an "as soon as I can" action is by the particular context required—the tool, location, or situation needed to complete it. If you have fifty or a hundred next actions, keeping them on one big list makes it too difficult to see what you need to see.

### Common Context Categories

- **Calls**: Record the phone number alongside each item. Many situations exist where you'd make the call if the number was already there but not if you had to look it up.
- **At Computer**: Group all actions requiring the computer to be on and running. Allen maintains a separate Online action list for when he's on a plane without Wi-Fi.
- **Errands**: Group together reminders of things you need to do when you're out. Sublists within individual Errands items are helpful—"hardware store" could be the list item with a sublist of all things to pick up there.
- **At Office**: For actions requiring physical presence there, such as purging a filing cabinet or printing a large document with a staff person.
- **At Home**: Many actions can be done only at home. If you work only at home, the At Home list could suffice.
- **Agendas**: Many next actions need to occur in real-time interaction with someone or be brought up in a meeting. Professionals who keep a file folder for things to go over with their boss already use a version of this method. You may need between three and fifteen of these lists. Standing meetings deserve their own lists.
- **Read/Review**: Printed items demanding more than two minutes are best managed in a separate physical stack tray. The pile must be reserved only for those longer-than-two-minute things you actually want to read.

### Organizing "Waiting For"

Reminders of things you're waiting to get back from others need to be sorted and grouped. You won't be tracking discrete action steps here, but final deliverables or projects others are responsible for. When the next action is up to someone else, you don't need an action reminder—just a trigger about what you're waiting for and from whom. Include the date each item was requested and any agreed-upon due date. Follow-up is much more meaningful when you can say, "But I placed the order March twentieth."

### Using Original Items as Reminders

Some paper-based materials and some e-mail most efficiently serve as their own reminders. For paper: Read/Review articles go in the tray themselves. If doing paper-based bill paying, keep bills in a folder labeled "Bills to Pay." Receipts for expense reporting should be kept in their own Receipts to Process envelope. For e-mail: Allen recommends creating folders titled "@ACTION" and "@WAITING FOR" with prefix symbols so they sort to the top of the navigator bar. When you delegate via e-mail, save a cc: or bcc: copy into your @WAITING FOR folder. It takes much less energy to maintain e-mail backlog at zero than at a thousand.

### Caution About Dispersing Reminders

Distributing action triggers in folders, on lists, and/or in an e-mail system is fine as long as you review all categories equally as required. Your @ACTION folder is an extension of your At Computer list and should be handled in exactly the same fashion. The digital world can be dangerous because as soon as data is offscreen, it can disappear as a viable prompt.

## Organizing Project Reminders

Creating and maintaining one list of all your projects (more than one action needed to achieve a desired result) can be a profound experience. You probably have more of them than you think.

### Value of a Complete Projects List

- **Critical for control and focus**: It is impossible to be truly relaxed and in your productive state when things you've told yourself you need to handle continue to pull at your mind.
- **Alleviates subtle tensions**: Projects seldom show up in nice, neat packages. Small things often slip unexpectedly into bigger things.
- **Core of the Weekly Review**: A complete Projects list remains the linchpin for that orientation.
- **Facilitates relationship management**: Being able to negotiate implicit and explicit agreements is the only way to effectively relieve inherent pressures.

### Where to Look for Hidden Projects

1. **Current activities**: What meetings are on your calendar because of some outcome you're committed to achieving? Many times people have "Call Mario re: the fund-raising event" on their Calls list but have not identified "Finalize the fund-raiser" as a project.
2. **Higher-horizon interests and commitments**: Review accountabilities you're invested in professionally. Are there things coming toward you further out that have started to pull on your attention?
3. **Current problems, issues, and opportunities**: When is a problem a project? Always. "Look into improving Frederick's relationship with his school" and "Resolve situation with landlord and building maintenance" are very real projects.

### One List or Subdivided?

Most people find that one list is best because it serves as a master inventory rather than a daily prioritizing guideline. However, it doesn't matter how many different lists you have, so long as you look at the contents of all of them as often as you need to. Common subdivisions include Personal/Professional, Delegated Projects, Specific Types of Projects, and Major Areas of Focus.

### Subprojects

If you're moving into a new residence and have subprojects like "Finalize the patio," "Upgrade the kitchen," and "Set up home office space," you could make "Upgrade new residence" one entry on your Projects list with subprojects in project support material. Allen notes: "As I write this, I'm in the throes of moving from California to Europe. For many months, I maintained one project on my Projects list: 'Move to Amsterdam.' Last week, as things became more immediate, I unpacked that one project into fifteen—all of which I need to keep my eyes on weekly now."

### Project Support Materials

Project support materials are not project actions and not project reminders—they're resources to support your actions and thinking. Don't use support materials as reminders. People use stacks of paper and stuffed file folders as reminders that they've got a project, but next actions haven't been determined. Files like that deliver an incessant subliminal chant: "Do something about me! Decide something about me!" When it's time to actually do an action, like making a call, you can pull out all the materials you think you might need.

## Organizing Nonactionable Data

### Reference Materials

Much of what comes across your desk is reference material with no action required. Your major decisions will be how much to keep, how much room to dedicate to it, what form it should be stored in, and where. When you've fully implemented this action-management methodology, you can be as big a pack rat as your space will allow. Most people wind up needing from one to four physical file drawers, many dozens of e-mail reference folders, and other digital storage locations. Reference systems include: General-reference filing (paper, e-mail, simple digital storage), Large-category filing (any topic requiring more than fifty folders), Contact managers, and Libraries and archives. The only issue with reference material is whether it's worth the time and space to keep it.

### Someday/Maybes

Someday/Maybes are not throwaway items. They may be some of the most interesting and creative things you'll ever get involved with. Activating and maintaining this category unleashes the flow of creative thinking—you have permission to imagine cool things without having to commit to doing anything about them yet. Allen notes that learning to play the flute and how to sail in the open ocean started in this category for him.

**Sources for Someday/Maybe items:**

- Your creative imagination: Things to get or build for your home, hobbies to take up, skills to learn, creative expressions to explore, trips to take, organizations to join, service projects to contribute to
- Your list of current projects: Review your Projects list from an elevated perspective and consider transferring optional projects

**Special categories** include Food (recipes, menus, restaurants, wines), Children (things to do with them), Books to read, Music to download, Movies to see, Gift ideas, Web sites to explore, Weekend trips to take.

**Danger of "Hold and Review" files**: Many people have created "Hold and Review" piles that vaguely fit within Someday/Maybe, but in virtually every case, the person held but didn't review. After appropriately processing someone's "Hold and Review" drawer, Allen discovered there was nothing left in it.

### Using the Calendar for Future Options

One of the three uses of a calendar is for day-specific information. This category can include triggers for activating projects, events you might want to participate in, and decision catalysts. It's OK to decide not to decide—as long as you have a decide-not-to-decide system.

### The Tickler File

The tickler file is a three-dimensional version of a calendar allowing you to hold physical reminders of things you want to see in the future. It allows you to in effect set up your own postal service and "mail" things to yourself for receipt on a designated future date. The tickler file demands only a one-second-per-day new behavior to make it work, and it has a payoff value exponentially greater than the personal investment. It represents a unique executive function: deciding not to decide until a certain point.

**Setting up a tickler file**: You need forty-three folders—thirty-one labeled "1" through "31," and twelve labeled with the months of the year. The daily files are kept in front, beginning with tomorrow's date. Behind the "31" file is the monthly file for the next month. When the next monthly file reaches the front, it's emptied into the in-tray and refiled at the back to represent that month a year from now. This is a perpetual file, meaning at any given time it contains files for the next thirty-one days and the next twelve months.

## Checklists: Creative and Constructive Reminders

Alfred North Whitehead observed: "Civilization advances by extending the number of important operations which we can perform without thinking about them." Checklists provide the micro version of that macro observation. Whenever you have to think about anything because of some regularity or a specific situation requiring more detail than you can easily recall, you should entrust those jobs to your "external mind."

### Things You Want to Pay Attention To

Often what shows up are things like "Exercise more regularly," "Spend more quality time with my kids," or "Maintain good morale on my team." For much of this, there is still a project and/or action that needs to be defined. "Exercise more regularly" translates into "Set up regular exercise program" (project) and "Call Sally for suggestion about gyms and personal trainers" (action step).

### Blueprinting Key Areas

A complete inventory of everything you hold important and are committed to could include: Career goals, Service, Family, Relationships, Community, Health and energy, Financial resources, Creative expression. The more novel the situation, the more control required. If you've been doing what you're doing for a long time with no pressure to change, you probably need minimal external personal organization to stay on cruise control.

### Checklists at All Levels

Examples of useful checklists: Job Areas of Responsibility, Exercise Regimens, Travel Checklist, Weekly Review, Training Program Components, Key Clients, People to Stay in Touch With, Year-end Activities, Personal Development, Jokes. Capability and willingness to instantly make a checklist, accessible and used when needed, is a core component of high-performance self-management.

# Organizing: Setting Up the Right Buckets

## Core Organizing Principle

Being organized means where something is matches what it means to you. If you decide to keep something as reference and put it where reference material belongs, that's organized. Your physical organization system must be better than your mental one for your mind to let go of lower-level thinking.

## The Seven Basic Categories

Seven primary types of things to keep track of:

1. A Projects list
2. Project support material
3. Calendar actions and information
4. Next Actions lists
5. A Waiting For list
6. Reference material
7. A Someday/Maybe list

### Hard Edges

Categories must be kept visually, physically, and psychologically separate. If you allow things of different meanings into the same grouping, you go psychologically numb to the contents. If you put items on Next Actions lists that need to go on the calendar, you won't trust your calendar. Projects you're not acting on must go on Someday/Maybe.

### Lists and Folders

Once you know what you need to track, lists and folders are sufficient tools. A list could be: a file folder with separate notes, an actual list on paper, or an inventory in software.

## Organizing Action Reminders

After emptying your in-tray, you'll have twenty to seventy or more pending items representing longer-than-two-minute actions that cannot be delegated.

### Calendar Actions

The calendar should show only the "hard landscape." There are two kinds of actions: those that must be done on a certain day and/or at a particular time, and those that just need to be done as soon as you can. Resist putting on the calendar things you'd like to get done but that might not happen. You need to trust your calendar as sacred territory.

### Organizing Actions by Context

The best way to be reminded of an "as soon as I can" action is by the particular context required—the tool, location, or situation needed to complete it. If you have fifty or a hundred next actions, keeping them on one big list makes it too difficult to see what you need to see.

### Common Context Categories

- **Calls**: Record the phone number alongside each item. Many situations exist where you'd make the call if the number was already there but not if you had to look it up.
- **At Computer**: Group all actions requiring the computer to be on and running. Allen maintains a separate Online action list for when he's on a plane without Wi-Fi.
- **Errands**: Group together reminders of things you need to do when you're out. Sublists within individual Errands items are helpful—"hardware store" could be the list item with a sublist of all things to pick up there.
- **At Office**: For actions requiring physical presence there, such as purging a filing cabinet or printing a large document with a staff person.
- **At Home**: Many actions can be done only at home. If you work only at home, the At Home list could suffice.
- **Agendas**: Many next actions need to occur in real-time interaction with someone or be brought up in a meeting. Professionals who keep a file folder for things to go over with their boss already use a version of this method. You may need between three and fifteen of these lists. Standing meetings deserve their own lists.
- **Read/Review**: Printed items demanding more than two minutes are best managed in a separate physical stack tray. The pile must be reserved only for those longer-than-two-minute things you actually want to read.

### Organizing "Waiting For"

Reminders of things you're waiting to get back from others need to be sorted and grouped. You won't be tracking discrete action steps here, but final deliverables or projects others are responsible for. When the next action is up to someone else, you don't need an action reminder—just a trigger about what you're waiting for and from whom. Include the date each item was requested and any agreed-upon due date. Follow-up is much more meaningful when you can say, "But I placed the order March twentieth."

### Using Original Items as Reminders

Some paper-based materials and some e-mail most efficiently serve as their own reminders. For paper: Read/Review articles go in the tray themselves. If doing paper-based bill paying, keep bills in a folder labeled "Bills to Pay." Receipts for expense reporting should be kept in their own Receipts to Process envelope. For e-mail: Allen recommends creating folders titled "@ACTION" and "@WAITING FOR" with prefix symbols so they sort to the top of the navigator bar. When you delegate via e-mail, save a cc: or bcc: copy into your @WAITING FOR folder. It takes much less energy to maintain e-mail backlog at zero than at a thousand.

### Caution About Dispersing Reminders

Distributing action triggers in folders, on lists, and/or in an e-mail system is fine as long as you review all categories equally as required. Your @ACTION folder is an extension of your At Computer list and should be handled in exactly the same fashion. The digital world can be dangerous because as soon as data is offscreen, it can disappear as a viable prompt.

## Organizing Project Reminders

Creating and maintaining one list of all your projects (more than one action needed to achieve a desired result) can be a profound experience. You probably have more of them than you think.

### Value of a Complete Projects List

- **Critical for control and focus**: It is impossible to be truly relaxed and in your productive state when things you've told yourself you need to handle continue to pull at your mind.
- **Alleviates subtle tensions**: Projects seldom show up in nice, neat packages. Small things often slip unexpectedly into bigger things.
- **Core of the Weekly Review**: A complete Projects list remains the linchpin for that orientation.
- **Facilitates relationship management**: Being able to negotiate implicit and explicit agreements is the only way to effectively relieve inherent pressures.

### Where to Look for Hidden Projects

1. **Current activities**: What meetings are on your calendar because of some outcome you're committed to achieving? Many times people have "Call Mario re: the fund-raising event" on their Calls list but have not identified "Finalize the fund-raiser" as a project.
2. **Higher-horizon interests and commitments**: Review accountabilities you're invested in professionally. Are there things coming toward you further out that have started to pull on your attention?
3. **Current problems, issues, and opportunities**: When is a problem a project? Always. "Look into improving Frederick's relationship with his school" and "Resolve situation with landlord and building maintenance" are very real projects.

### One List or Subdivided?

Most people find that one list is best because it serves as a master inventory rather than a daily prioritizing guideline. However, it doesn't matter how many different lists you have, so long as you look at the contents of all of them as often as you need to. Common subdivisions include Personal/Professional, Delegated Projects, Specific Types of Projects, and Major Areas of Focus.

### Subprojects

If you're moving into a new residence and have subprojects like "Finalize the patio," "Upgrade the kitchen," and "Set up home office space," you could make "Upgrade new residence" one entry on your Projects list with subprojects in project support material. Allen notes: "As I write this, I'm in the throes of moving from California to Europe. For many months, I maintained one project on my Projects list: 'Move to Amsterdam.' Last week, as things became more immediate, I unpacked that one project into fifteen—all of which I need to keep my eyes on weekly now."

### Project Support Materials

Project support materials are not project actions and not project reminders—they're resources to support your actions and thinking. Don't use support materials as reminders. People use stacks of paper and stuffed file folders as reminders that they've got a project, but next actions haven't been determined. Files like that deliver an incessant subliminal chant: "Do something about me! Decide something about me!" When it's time to actually do an action, like making a call, you can pull out all the materials you think you might need.

## Organizing Nonactionable Data

### Reference Materials

Much of what comes across your desk is reference material with no action required. Your major decisions will be how much to keep, how much room to dedicate to it, what form it should be stored in, and where. When you've fully implemented this action-management methodology, you can be as big a pack rat as your space will allow. Most people wind up needing from one to four physical file drawers, many dozens of e-mail reference folders, and other digital storage locations. Reference systems include: General-reference filing (paper, e-mail, simple digital storage), Large-category filing (any topic requiring more than fifty folders), Contact managers, and Libraries and archives. The only issue with reference material is whether it's worth the time and space to keep it.

### Someday/Maybes

Someday/Maybes are not throwaway items. They may be some of the most interesting and creative things you'll ever get involved with. Activating and maintaining this category unleashes the flow of creative thinking—you have permission to imagine cool things without having to commit to doing anything about them yet. Allen notes that learning to play the flute and how to sail in the open ocean started in this category for him.

**Sources for Someday/Maybe items:**

- Your creative imagination: Things to get or build for your home, hobbies to take up, skills to learn, creative expressions to explore, trips to take, organizations to join, service projects to contribute to
- Your list of current projects: Review your Projects list from an elevated perspective and consider transferring optional projects

**Special categories** include Food (recipes, menus, restaurants, wines), Children (things to do with them), Books to read, Music to download, Movies to see, Gift ideas, Web sites to explore, Weekend trips to take.

**Danger of "Hold and Review" files**: Many people have created "Hold and Review" piles that vaguely fit within Someday/Maybe, but in virtually every case, the person held but didn't review. After appropriately processing someone's "Hold and Review" drawer, Allen discovered there was nothing left in it.

### Using the Calendar for Future Options

One of the three uses of a calendar is for day-specific information. This category can include triggers for activating projects, events you might want to participate in, and decision catalysts. It's OK to decide not to decide—as long as you have a decide-not-to-decide system.

### The Tickler File

The tickler file is a three-dimensional version of a calendar allowing you to hold physical reminders of things you want to see in the future. It allows you to in effect set up your own postal service and "mail" things to yourself for receipt on a designated future date. The tickler file demands only a one-second-per-day new behavior to make it work, and it has a payoff value exponentially greater than the personal investment. It represents a unique executive function: deciding not to decide until a certain point.

**Setting up a tickler file**: You need forty-three folders—thirty-one labeled "1" through "31," and twelve labeled with the months of the year. The daily files are kept in front, beginning with tomorrow's date. Behind the "31" file is the monthly file for the next month. When the next monthly file reaches the front, it's emptied into the in-tray and refiled at the back to represent that month a year from now. This is a perpetual file, meaning at any given time it contains files for the next thirty-one days and the next twelve months.

## Checklists: Creative and Constructive Reminders

Alfred North Whitehead observed: "Civilization advances by extending the number of important operations which we can perform without thinking about them." Checklists provide the micro version of that macro observation. Whenever you have to think about anything because of some regularity or a specific situation requiring more detail than you can easily recall, you should entrust those jobs to your "external mind."

### Things You Want to Pay Attention To

Often what shows up are things like "Exercise more regularly," "Spend more quality time with my kids," or "Maintain good morale on my team." For much of this, there is still a project and/or action that needs to be defined. "Exercise more regularly" translates into "Set up regular exercise program" (project) and "Call Sally for suggestion about gyms and personal trainers" (action step).

### Blueprinting Key Areas

A complete inventory of everything you hold important and are committed to could include: Career goals, Service, Family, Relationships, Community, Health and energy, Financial resources, Creative expression. The more novel the situation, the more control required. If you've been doing what you're doing for a long time with no pressure to change, you probably need minimal external personal organization to stay on cruise control.

### Checklists at All Levels

Examples of useful checklists: Job Areas of Responsibility, Exercise Regimens, Travel Checklist, Weekly Review, Training Program Components, Key Clients, People to Stay in Touch With, Year-end Activities, Personal Development, Jokes. Capability and willingness to instantly make a checklist, accessible and used when needed, is a core component of high-performance self-management.
